generatedProse.concept-context: Practice and work-based learning is hard to assess with a standard exam, because one placement, one studio and one field project each ask for different work. So tutors assess what you can show you learned, usually through a reflective account, a portfolio or a report. The grade follows the quality of your evidence, not how busy the experience looked. That makes one distinction decisive: describing what happened earns little, while showing what you learned, tied to a specific moment and to what you would do next, is what gains marks.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students writing up the same placement for assessment.

Student A describes the weeks in order: the tasks done, the people met, the sessions watched. It is accurate and complete, and it reads like a diary. But it stays at the level of what happened, so a marker learns what Student A did without learning what Student A took from it.

Student B picks a few moments that taught something and builds on each. One decision showed how the team weighed competing demands; Student B explains what that revealed and how it will change their own practice. The account is shorter on events but rich in learning.

Both did the same placement. Student B offered evidence of learning, where Student A offered only a record of activity.
generatedProse.summary: A practice or work-based experience is assessed on the learning you can show, not on the activity itself, which is why evidence beats description. You can now explain how the assessment works and why standard criteria are hard, tell evidence apart from description, and prepare strong evidence of your own. With aims set, the experience worked actively, and your learning evidenced, you are ready to make the most of whatever practice your course brings.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Student B's write-up stronger evidence than Student A's?

items.text: Student B showed what they learned from specific moments and what they would change, rather than listing what happened.
Student B covered more of the weeks in greater detail.
Student B wrote more neatly and with fewer errors.
Student B quoted the supervisor's praise of the placement.

feedback.correct: That's right. Student B showed learning from specific moments, and what they would change, which is what makes it evidence.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Student B showed beyond what happened.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Student B's write-up was stronger evidence because it showed learning from specific moments and what they would change, rather than listing events, polishing the prose or quoting praise.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; name the cast directly in the prose (the pack supplies the whole body). The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
